analysis.one_liner: Diverts Social Security trust fund surpluses into personal investment accounts, reducing guaranteed benefits and exempting accounts from estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote in the Senate Finance Committee, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have taken the yearly surplus in the Social Security trust fund — money that now goes into government bonds — and instead deposited it into a personal investment account for every worker born in 1950 or later. Workers could invest in government securities and, starting in 2008, broad index funds like those in the federal employee retirement plan. At retirement, traditional monthly benefits would be reduced by an amount tied to what the account earned, and any leftover account balance would go to the worker's heirs tax-free. Supporters pitched it as locking Social Security money away from other government spending; critics of privatization noted it shifts retirement risk from a guaranteed benefit to stock and bond markets while routing the money through private fund managers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers born in 1950 or later would get an account in their own name, invested in government securities or index funds, with any remaining balance passing to a spouse or heirs at death. Certified private account managers would hold and invest the money, earning administration fees of up to 0.30% of assets per year. Estates would gain because account assets would be exempt from the estate tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with accounts and fund managers

how_it_helps.text: Each participating worker would get a personal retirement account funded by a share of the yearly Social Security trust fund surplus, proportional to their wages [S2] [S3].
Accounts would be invested in a mix of U.S. government securities, with broad-based index funds similar to the federal Thrift Savings Plan available starting in 2008 [S2] [S3].
Account assets would pass to a surviving spouse, a designated person, or the estate when a participant dies, rather than disappearing with the benefit [S3].
The bill guarantees that traditional benefits plus the account would together provide at least a poverty-level retirement income, buying an annuity if needed [S3].
Account balances would be exempt from income tax and from the estate tax [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury general fund would have to make transfers to keep the trust funds at 100 percent of the year's benefit obligations through 2041, adding to federal borrowing needs. Workers would bear market risk: monthly traditional benefits would be reduced by a formula tied to what their account would have earned, so a poorly performing market means a smaller combined retirement income. The fund managers' fees, though capped at 30 basis points, would come out of account balances.

drawbacks.text: Traditional Social Security checks would be reduced by an offset formula tied to hypothetical account earnings, meaning workers take on market risk that the current system spreads across generations [S3].

The Treasury would be required to transfer general revenue to keep both trust funds fully funded through 2041, a cost the bill's own findings acknowledge should be temporary and eventually repaid [S2] [S3].

Administrative fees charged by certified account managers — up to 0.30% of assets per year — would be deducted from account balances, reducing returns compared with the trust fund's current structure [S3].
The estate tax exemption for account assets is a tax benefit that accrues to heirs of account holders with the largest balances [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives workers a property right in an account that can be inherited, and guarantees at least a poverty-level combined retirement income. But the offset formula means the account largely substitutes for benefits workers would have received anyway, so the net gain depends entirely on investment returns outperforming the trust fund — while the general-revenue transfers required to keep the trust funds whole shift the financing burden to taxpayers. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the plan's fiscal math depends on the surplus staying large enough to fund meaningful accounts, and that it does not address Social Security's long-term financing shortfall.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint and eleven Republican colleagues introduced the bill in the Senate on June 23, 2005 [S1] [S4] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress; the only later entry is a repeat of the sponsor's introductory remarks in November 2005 [S5] [S1].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and bills not passed by then expire [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any action, the traditional Social Security structure — a guaranteed benefit financed by the trust fund — remained unchanged, and private fund managers did not gain a new mandated channel for Social Security surpluses. Opponents of privatizing Social Security surpluses were better off; the bill's sponsors gained nothing beyond the introduction itself.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support; the bill then died in a Republican-chaired committee without ever reaching the floor.

industries.industry: Asset management and mutual fund industry
industries.note: Certified private account managers would have taken over investment of Social Security surpluses for every worker born after 1949, collecting administration fees of up to 0.30% of assets per year. The industry's gain would have come from replacing a government-run trust fund with a permanent private fee stream funded by workers' payroll taxes.

Account assets would have been exempt from the estate tax, a benefit that grows with the size of the account and disproportionately helps larger estates. The exemption would reduce estate tax revenue that now applies to inherited wealth.

At retirement, account balances would have been used to purchase life annuities guaranteeing at least a poverty-level income, creating a large new annuity market. Consumers would be buying a product that guarantees a floor they could otherwise fall below, though annuity pricing would determine how much value they get.
